def: Transition (d-block) elements have the general electronic configuration (n-1)d(1-10) ns(0-2), where the outer s-orbital and the inner d-orbital are both partly filled.
points: Transition elements lie between s-block and p-block, in groups 3 to 12 of the periodic table.
3d series (Sc to Zn) fills the 3d orbitals while the 4s orbital is already filled or nearly filled.
Exceptions occur due to extra stability of half-filled and fully-filled d-orbitals: Cr is 3d5 4s1 and Cu is 3d10 4s1, not the expected 3d4 4s2 or 3d9 4s2.
Zn, Cd, Hg have fully filled d10 configuration and are often excluded from typical transition metal behaviour since they do not have incomplete d-orbitals.
During ionisation, electrons are lost first from the 4s orbital before the 3d orbital.
This (n-1)d ns arrangement explains variable oxidation states and other transition metal properties.

diagram.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  A["Fill 1s to 4s orbitals normally"] --> B["Start filling 3d orbitals"]
  B --> C["Exceptions: Cr = 3d5 4s1"]
  C --> D["Exceptions: Cu = 3d10 4s1"]
  D --> E["Zn = 3d10 4s2, fully filled d"]

example: Electronic configuration of Fe (Z=26): [Ar] 3d6 4s2. Fe2+ loses two 4s electrons: [Ar] 3d6. Fe3+ loses one more from 3d: [Ar] 3d5.
tip: Always write configurations of Cr and Cu correctly with the exception noted — these are favourite one-mark questions.

def: Transition elements show several oxidation states in their compounds because the energies of (n-1)d and ns electrons are very close, so both can take part in bonding.
points: Since (n-1)d and ns orbitals have similar energy, electrons from both can be removed with comparable ease.
This gives a range of oxidation states differing usually by one unit, e.g. Fe2+ and Fe3+, Mn2+ to Mn7+.
Lower oxidation states are more ionic in character; higher oxidation states are more covalent.
The most stable (common) oxidation state is usually +2 for most 3d metals, arising from loss of the two 4s electrons.
Manganese shows the widest range of oxidation states (+2 to +7) among 3d elements due to its half-filled d5 configuration at +2.
Compounds in higher oxidation states, such as MnO4- and CrO4(2-), are often strong oxidising agents.
formula: Common oxidation states differ by units of one, e.g. Fe: +2, +3; Mn: +2 to +7

diagram.mermaid:
flowchart TD
  A["(n-1)d and ns close in energy"] --> B["Both sets of electrons can be removed"]
  B --> C["Multiple oxidation states possible"]
  C --> D["Higher states more covalent and oxidising"]
  C --> E["Lower states more ionic"]

example: Manganese shows +2 (Mn2+), +4 (MnO2), +6 (MnO4 2-) and +7 (MnO4-) oxidation states, with KMnO4 (+7) being a powerful oxidising agent.
tip: Quote manganese as the best example of maximum oxidation states and explain the +2 state using the 4s2 electron loss.

t: Magnetic Properties and Colour of Ions
def: Transition metal ions are often coloured and magnetic because of unpaired electrons in their incompletely filled d-orbitals.
points: Paramagnetism arises when an ion has one or more unpaired electrons; they are attracted into a magnetic field.
Magnetic moment increases with the number of unpaired electrons: mu = sqrt(n(n+2)) Bohr magneton, where n is number of unpaired electrons.
Ions with no unpaired electrons (like Zn2+, d10) are diamagnetic and show no colour.
Colour arises from d-d transitions: an electron absorbs visible light to jump from a lower-energy d-orbital to a higher-energy d-orbital, and the complementary colour is seen.
Ions with completely empty (d0) or completely filled (d10) d-orbitals usually show no colour because no d-d transition is possible.
Colour and magnetic behaviour both depend directly on the number of unpaired d-electrons present.
formula: mu = sqrt(n(n+2)) Bohr magneton, where n = number of unpaired electrons

diagram.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  A["Ion has unpaired d electrons"] --> B["Paramagnetic behaviour"]
  A --> C["Light absorbed for d-d transition"]
  C --> D["Ion appears coloured"]
  E["No unpaired electrons, d0 or d10"] --> F["Diamagnetic and colourless"]

example: Ti3+ (3d1) has 1 unpaired electron, mu = sqrt(1x3) = 1.73 BM, and appears violet/purple due to a single d-d transition.
tip: Always connect colour and magnetism to the same cause: unpaired d-electrons. State clearly when an ion is colourless (d0/d10).

def: Many transition metals and their compounds act as good catalysts because of their ability to show variable oxidation states and to form unstable intermediate compounds with reactants.
points: Variable oxidation states allow transition metals to accept and donate electrons easily, helping redox reactions proceed.
They can form intermediate complexes with reactants, providing a new, lower-energy pathway for the reaction.
Large surface area (in finely divided or powdered metal form) increases adsorption of reactant molecules, improving catalytic action.
Vacant d-orbitals allow reactant molecules to bind to the metal surface and get activated (weakening bonds for easier reaction).
Examples: Fe catalyses the Haber process for ammonia; V2O5 catalyses SO2 to SO3 oxidation in the Contact process; Ni catalyses hydrogenation of oils.
formula: Catalysis via variable oxidation state: M(n+) <-> M((n+2)+) + 2e- (electron transfer cycle)

diagram.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  A["Reactants adsorb on metal surface"] --> B["Form unstable intermediate with metal"]
  B --> C["Lower activation energy pathway"]
  C --> D["Products formed and released"]
  D --> E["Catalyst surface regenerated"]

example: In the Contact process, V2O5 first gets reduced by SO2 to V2O4, then V2O4 is reoxidised by O2 back to V2O5, repeatedly converting SO2 to SO3.
tip: Give at least two named industrial examples (Fe in Haber process, V2O5 in Contact process) for full marks.

def: Lanthanoid contraction is the steady and gradual decrease in atomic and ionic radii of the lanthanoid series elements as atomic number increases from La to Lu.
points: As atomic number increases across lanthanoids, electrons are added to the inner 4f orbitals.
4f orbitals have poor shielding effect compared to d or p orbitals, so the increasing nuclear charge is not effectively screened.
This poor shielding causes the effective nuclear charge felt by outer electrons to increase, pulling the outer shell closer and shrinking the atomic/ionic radius.
The cumulative effect across all 14 lanthanoids is called lanthanoid contraction.
It causes the radii of elements just after the lanthanoids (like Zr and Hf, or Nb and Ta) to become almost similar, making their separation difficult.
This similarity of post-lanthanoid elements is a direct consequence used to explain near-identical properties of 4d and 5d congeners.
formula: Radius decrease per element is small, but cumulative decrease across 14 lanthanoids is significant (~ 20 pm smaller overall)

diagram.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  A["Electrons added to 4f orbitals"] --> B["Poor shielding by 4f electrons"]
  B --> C["Increased effective nuclear charge"]
  C --> D["Outer shell pulled closer to nucleus"]
  D --> E["Gradual decrease in radius: lanthanoid contraction"]

example: Because of lanthanoid contraction, Zr (atomic radius ~160 pm) and Hf (~159 pm) have almost identical radii, making their chemical separation very difficult.
tip: Explain the cause (poor 4f shielding) and one consequence (similar radii of Zr/Hf or Nb/Ta) — both parts are usually required for full marks.

def: Actinoids are the 14 elements following actinium (atomic numbers 90-103) in which the 5f orbitals are progressively filled; they are mostly radioactive and show more variable oxidation states than lanthanoids.
points: General electronic configuration: (n-2)f(1-14) (n-1)d(0-1) ns2, with filling of 5f orbitals.
All actinoids are radioactive; many are synthetic (man-made) and unstable, especially those after uranium (transuranium elements).

+3 is the common oxidation state, similar to lanthanoids, but actinoids show a wider range of oxidation states (e.g. +3 to +7 for some elements like uranium and neptunium) because 5f, 6d and 7s orbitals are close in energy.
Actinoid contraction also occurs (radii decrease across the series) similar to lanthanoid contraction, but it is less regular due to greater involvement of 6d orbitals.
Actinoids are harder to study because many are radioactive, short-lived, and available only in very small (sometimes trace) quantities.
Compared to lanthanoids, actinoid compounds show more covalent character due to greater involvement of 5f, 6d electrons in bonding.
formula: General configuration: (n-2)f^1-14 (n-1)d^0-1 ns^2; common oxidation state +3

diagram.mermaid:
flowchart TD
  A["Actinoids, Z = 90 to 103"] --> B["5f orbitals progressively filled"]
  B --> C["Mostly radioactive elements"]
  C --> D["Wider range of oxidation states than lanthanoids"]
  D --> E["Actinoid contraction similar to lanthanoid contraction"]

example: Uranium shows oxidation states from +3 to +6 (commonly +6 in UO2 2+, uranyl ion), unlike most lanthanoids which are mainly restricted to +3.
tip: Contrast actinoids with lanthanoids on three points: radioactivity, wider oxidation states, and greater covalent character — a standard comparison question.
